before: Now when the sun had set and darkness was over the land, Nestor said, "It is getting late; it is time we were all in bed. The libations have been made and the prayers offered; let us go home to rest." Thus he spoke, and they did exactly as he said, yoking the swift horses to the chariot. The housekeeper packed them provisions of bread, wine, and delicacies fit for princes. Then Telemachus got into the chariot while Pisistratus gathered up the reins and took the seat beside him. He whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly into the open country, leaving the high citadel of Pylos behind them. All day they traveled, with the yoke swaying on their necks, until the sun set and darkness covered the land. Then they reached Pherae, where Diocles lived—son of Ortilochus and grandson of Alpheus. Here they spent the night, and Diocles entertained them hospitably. When rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, they again harnessed their horses and drove out through the gateway under the echoing portico. Pisistratus whipped the horses on, and they flew forward eagerly. Soon they came to the wheat lands of the open country, and in due time completed their journey, so well did their steeds carry them.
